title: Tales of Genetics: Aquatic Twat
summary: NH tells his own story as a naturally gifted child swimmer who became arrogant, quit training, and was humiliated in a school swimming exam by trained competitive swimmers. He gassed out after the first 25 m and had to be dragged out of the pool. The lesson: hard work beats talent when talent doesn't work hard, and a lack of genetic gifts can be an advantage because it makes you a grinder.
claims: NH is not gifted for bodybuilding but was a natural swimming talent
At two NH nearly drowned yet was instinctively doing breaststroke; he was swimming by three or four
Before age 10 NH could swim an Olympic pool length underwater on one breath
His talent made NH arrogant; he belittled other kids and his instructors never disciplined him because they wanted to win
Moved up to train with 12-13-year-olds at 10, NH quit when forced into structured laps, thinking he was already the best
As a teen NH swam big waves on the island's most dangerous beach and beat fit adults without training
Untrained for two years, NH entered a school 4x25 m competition against trained swimmers and went all out on the first length
He led after 25 m, was last after 50 m, finished alone with cramps and had to be dragged out
The public humiliation taught NH humility, which he sees as essential to growing up
Talent that isn't developed is wasted; in the balance, hard work outweighs genetics
Hard work beats talent when talent doesn't work hard
A kid NH mocked at nine kept training for years and beat him in that exam
What matters is how you play the cards you're dealt, not the cards themselves
Some people would have done better with less talent, because easy success kills the drive to work
Having poor genetics can be a gift because it forces you to become a grinder
